implementation_notes: CompletableFuture is the Java 8 realization: supplyAsync per part (async methods without an executor use ForkJoinPool.commonPool), a List<CompletableFuture<Result>> as the correlation state, CompletableFuture.allOf(...) as the completion barrier, then a stream over the futures that join()s and reduces the results into the reply. The routing decision is a branch over the part type inside the supplier, so no separate router object is needed in-process; the classic Aggregator keeps its value when parts travel over JMS/Kafka and the state must be durable.
pitfalls: allOf().join() reports only the first failure as a CompletionException; a partial aggregate must inspect each future with handle()/isCompletedExceptionally().
Every async stage without an explicit executor shares ForkJoinPool.commonPool, so a blocking part (JDBC, HTTP) starves unrelated code in the same JVM - pass a dedicated executor.
join() inside the common pool's threads can deadlock when the pool is saturated by the very parts you are waiting for.

variants.name: StructuredTaskScope fork/join (Java 21 structured concurrency)
variants.implementation_notes: Java 21's structured concurrency maps the composite onto one lexical scope: fork one subtask per part, treat scope.join().throwIfFailed() as the completion barrier, then read each Subtask's value in part order and reduce; ShutdownOnFailure cancels the siblings on the first failure, and a custom scope overriding handleComplete is the documented extension point for partial results. The Oracle guide notes the API is a preview feature in Java 21 (compile with the preview flags), so the enclosed scope - and with it the composite - is guaranteed to finish before the enclosing task continues.
pitfalls: Subtask values belong to the scope: read them inside the try-with-resources block (the Oracle examples reduce inside), never after close().
throwIfFailed() is a fail-fast policy only; partial aggregation needs a custom scope that overrides handleComplete.
The API is a preview feature in Java 21: without the preview flags it does not compile, and its shape may change in later releases.
